decisions.reason: A metaethical family combines independently interpreted answers; one diagnostic case cannot identify a family.

construct.name: Metaethical family
construct.description: Derived classification over realist, constructivist, subjectivist, error-theoretic, noncognitivist, and related families.

candidateItems.text: Consider the claim that deceiving someone for amusement is morally wrong. Which description best fits your understanding of this kind of moral claim?

options.label: It can describe a moral fact independent of anyone’s approval.
It can be true or false relative to an individual’s standards.
It can be true or false relative to a cultural framework.
It purports to state a fact, but affirmative claims of moral rightness or wrongness are systematically false.
It primarily expresses an attitude or prescription rather than asserting a literal truth.
None of these descriptions fits my view.

decisions.reason: The original domination items are not an administration of MFQ-2 or a calibrated foundation.

construct.name: Liberty / opposition to domination
construct.description: Experimental moral-foundation construct concerning domination, coercion, and liberty.

candidateItems.text: When judging whether an arrangement is morally acceptable, how relevant is whether one person is subject to another's arbitrary control?
An arrangement can be morally objectionable because it places someone under another person's uncontrolled power even when material outcomes are good.
A worker receives high pay and good treatment but may be arbitrarily dismissed, searched, or reassigned at a superior's whim. How morally relevant is that vulnerability?

options.label: Very morally relevant because arbitrary power is itself objectionable.
Somewhat relevant, though good treatment matters strongly.
Only slightly relevant if the superior actually behaves well.
Not morally relevant unless the power is abused.

candidateItems.text: Being able to refuse, exit, or contest another person's control can itself be morally important.

academicSources.title: Atari et al. (2023): Morality Beyond the WEIRD: How the Nomological Network of Morality Varies Across Cultures
Iyer et al. (2012): Understanding Libertarian Morality

decisions.reason: The knowledge-structure items address complexity directly; use only that narrow proposition.

construct.name: Knowledge complexity
construct.description: Tendency to regard knowledge as complex, interconnected, and developing rather than simple and fixed.

candidateItems.text: Knowledge in complex fields is usually made of interconnected claims that can change as new evidence and concepts develop.
Most important questions have fairly simple answers once the relevant facts are known.
A field contains many well-supported findings, but new discoveries regularly change how those findings fit together. Which is closest to your view of knowledge in such a field?

options.label: Knowledge is a changing network of interconnected claims.
Most knowledge is stable, with only peripheral details changing.
Knowledge is mainly a collection of separate facts.
It depends heavily on the field.

academicSources.title: Schommer (1990): Effects of Beliefs About the Nature of Knowledge on Comprehension

answerMeanings.proposition: Knowledge in complex fields is interconnected and revisable as inquiry develops.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
falsePositives: Disagreeing that most questions are simple may reflect uncertainty rather than interconnected knowledge.

decisions.reason: The existing answer set confounds knowledge with certainty and domain-limited skepticism.

construct.name: Attainability of truth
construct.description: Confidence that objective truth or knowledge is attainable in principle.

candidateItems.text: For at least some questions, human inquiry can arrive at answers that are objectively correct rather than merely useful or conventional.
Some important questions may remain permanently beyond the limits of human knowledge.
Which description is closest to your view of human inquiry?

options.label: For many important questions, objectively correct answers are attainable.
We can often approach truth without ever being certain we have reached it.
Important domains may have objective truths that humans cannot reliably know.
In many important domains, what counts as an answer is mainly practical or conventional.

decisions.reason: New observation, all empirical support, and substantive knowledge differ; the existing pair is not converse evidence.

construct.name: Rational / a priori reliance
construct.description: Epistemic weight assigned to reason, conceptual analysis, or a priori justification.

candidateItems.text: Reasoning alone can sometimes justify knowledge without relying on new observation.
Without empirical evidence, reasoning alone cannot establish substantive facts about reality.
Which is the clearest case of something that can be justified without new observation?

options.label: A conclusion following from logic or conceptual relations.
A claim about an unfamiliar physical object.
A claim about a past event.
No substantive claim can be justified without observation.

decisions.reason: Public repeatable testing is directly compared with private unchecked methods.

construct.name: Scientific-method reliance
construct.description: Epistemic weight assigned to systematic scientific methods.

candidateItems.text: Methods that expose claims to systematic testing deserve more confidence than methods that cannot be checked in comparable ways.
A claim can deserve high confidence even when it cannot be tested by systematic empirical methods.
Two methods disagree. One produces public, repeatable tests; the other relies on private experiences that cannot be independently checked. Which deserves more confidence?

options.label: A: The publicly testable method.
B: The private-experience method.

answerMeanings.proposition: Public repeatable testing merits greater confidence than a comparably unsupported private method.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
nonEntailments: Science is the only source of knowledge
falsePositives: Confidence in science must not be read as denying every nonscientific justification.

decisions.reason: The items address factual warrant from sincere revelation without independent verification.

construct.name: Revelation as epistemic source
construct.description: Epistemic weight assigned to alleged divine or supernatural revelation.

candidateItems.text: A revelation believed to come from a divine or supernatural source can sometimes provide genuine knowledge.
A sincere experience interpreted as revelation should not by itself justify factual claims about the world.
A person sincerely believes they received a clear revelation from a divine source, but the experience cannot be independently verified. How much factual justification does the experience provide?

options.label: Substantial justification for the person.
Some justification, though independent support is still needed.
Little factual justification.
No factual justification by itself.

answerMeanings.proposition: A sincerely believed revelation can itself give some factual justification without independent verification.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
falsePositives: A little justification or a need for independent support is not full endorsement.

decisions.reason: Mind-independence can be interpreted; direct perception and external-world skepticism remain separate gaps.

construct.name: External-world stance
construct.description: Direct realism, indirect realism, idealism, skepticism, or related positions regarding the external world.

candidateItems.text: Which description is closest to your view of ordinary perception?

options.label: In perception we are directly aware of ordinary external objects.
We are directly aware of perceptual representations caused by external objects.
What we call physical objects are fundamentally mind-dependent or experiential.
Perception cannot establish that an external world exists.

candidateItems.text: You discover that all of your current experiences could be perfectly produced by a simulation. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Ordinary knowledge of an external world can survive that possibility.
The possibility weakens confidence but does not eliminate external-world knowledge.
It shows that ordinary experience cannot establish external-world knowledge.
None of these descriptions fits well.

candidateItems.text: The objects you perceive normally exist independently of your mind even though perception is mediated by sensory processes.
Which claim is closest to your view of the physical world?

options.label: It exists independently of minds and perception.
Some of its experienced structure depends on minds, though something external remains.
Its existence or basic structure is fundamentally mind-dependent.
We should suspend judgment about what exists beyond experience.

answerMeanings.proposition: Ordinary perceived objects exist independently of minds.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
falsePositives: An indirect-perception answer is compatible with an external world.

decisions.reason: Substantive, framework-relative, and merely verbal disputes are different; the existing frequency claims do not align.

construct.name: Metaontology
construct.description: Whether ontological disputes are substantive, deflationary, quantifier-relative, or otherwise construed.

candidateItems.text: Disputes about what exists can express substantive disagreements about reality, not merely different choices of language.
Two theories may appear to disagree about what exists while differing only in how they use words or quantifiers.
Which description is closest to your view of many ontological disputes?

options.label: They are usually substantive disputes about reality.
They often depend on the conceptual or linguistic framework being used.
Many are mainly verbal or practical choices with little deep fact at stake.
Some are substantive and others are largely verbal.

decisions.reason: Transformation cases can inform a synthesis, but one teleportation scenario does not define a scale.

construct.name: Identity under transformation
construct.description: Derived pattern across teleportation, copying, uploading, replacement, and continuity vignettes.

candidateItems.text: A machine scans you perfectly, destroys your body, and creates an exact functioning duplicate elsewhere with all your memories and dispositions. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: The duplicate is straightforwardly the same person.
Something important survives, but strict numerical identity is unclear or lost.
The duplicate is a new person despite the perfect continuity.
The answer depends on a further fact about persons or consciousness.
None of these descriptions fits well.

decisions.reason: Compatibilist conditions cannot be used as denials of free will by incompatibilists.

construct.name: Free-will belief
construct.description: Strength of belief that human agents possess free will.

candidateItems.text: Human beings sometimes exercise genuine control over which action they choose.
A person's choices can genuinely be their own even when those choices have prior causes.
Assume a person's choice results from their own stable values and reasoning in a world where every event has prior causes. Could that choice still be genuinely free?

options.label: Yes, genuine freedom can be compatible with that causal history.
Possibly, depending on the kind of causal control the person has.
No, genuine freedom requires more than being caused by the person's values and reasoning.
None of these descriptions fits well.

candidateItems.text: A choice can be genuinely free when it flows from the person's own reasons and values without external coercion, even if those reasons have causes.

decisions.reason: A manipulated action and causal explanation do not negate the possibility of desert in other actions.

construct.name: Moral-responsibility belief
construct.description: Strength of belief in basic or desert-entailing moral responsibility.

candidateItems.text: A person can sometimes deserve moral blame for an action even after every causal explanation of why they acted has been given.
If an action is fully explained by causes for which the person was never responsible, basic desert-based blame no longer makes sense.
A person's harmful action results from manipulation that shaped their motives without their awareness. How much basic moral blame does the person deserve?

options.label: Roughly the same basic blame as without the manipulation.
Some blame, but substantially reduced.
No basic desert-based blame, though other responses may still be justified.
It depends on whether the person could recognize and resist the manipulation.

candidateItems.text: A person's moral responsibility can depend on whether the action truly expressed their agency, not merely on whether the action caused harm.

decisions.reason: Capacity for altruism and frequency of benevolent action differ; disagreeing with often does not deny capacity.

construct.name: Baseline human benevolence
construct.description: Belief that humans are naturally capable of or inclined toward benevolence/cooperation.

candidateItems.text: Without coercion or reward, people are often naturally capable of sustained cooperation and concern for others.
People often help others simply because they care, even when no reward or punishment is involved.

Someone anonymously returns a lost wallet containing a large amount of money when there is no realistic chance of reward or punishment. How informative is this about ordinary human capacity for benevolence?

options.label: Strong evidence that people can act from genuine concern for others.
Some evidence, though other motives may still be involved.
Little evidence about general human benevolence.
No meaningful evidence; self-interest can explain such behavior.

decisions.reason: Self-interest, psychological egoism, and competition are distinct claims; the current items bundle them.

construct.name: Baseline human selfishness / competition
construct.description: Belief that humans are naturally inclined toward selfishness, rivalry, or competition.

candidateItems.text: Even under favorable institutions, self-interest and competition remain powerful default tendencies in human behavior.
Self-interest and competition are not unavoidable default tendencies in human behavior.
In a setting where cooperation is rewarded and exploitation is difficult, most people cooperate reliably. What does this suggest about human selfishness?

options.label: Self-interest remains the basic default; institutions merely redirect it.
Humans have both cooperative and selfish tendencies that institutions can amplify.
Cooperation can itself be a basic human tendency rather than a disguise for selfishness.
The scenario alone does not tell us much about baseline human nature.

academicSources.title: Murphy, Ackermann & Handgraaf (2011): Measuring Social Value Orientation

decisions.reason: Change in some dispositions can coexist with stability in others; the apparent opposites have different quantifiers.

construct.name: Human-nature mutability
construct.description: Belief that human traits and dispositions are substantially malleable.

candidateItems.text: Many important human dispositions can change substantially when environments, incentives, and institutions change.
Many basic human dispositions remain fairly stable even when social conditions change substantially.
A generation grows up under very different institutions and develops markedly different habits of trust, aggression, and cooperation. How much should this shift your view of human malleability?

options.label: Strongly; major human dispositions can be highly malleable.
Somewhat; environments matter but within substantial limits.
Little; deeper human dispositions remain mostly stable.
Not at all; the observed differences need another explanation.

academicSources.title: Levy, Stroessner & Dweck (1998): Stereotype Formation and Endorsement

decisions.reason: Multicausal explanation is an exploratory methodological variable, not an interpreted human-nature factor.

construct.name: Human-nature complexity
construct.description: Belief that behavior resists simple, single-cause accounts.

candidateItems.text: Important human behavior usually results from several interacting causes rather than one dominant kind of cause.
Most important human behavior can be explained adequately by one or two dominant kinds of cause.
A person's aggression, trust, and risk-taking each change under different biological, social, and situational influences. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Human behavior is usually multiply caused and difficult to reduce to one explanatory dimension.
Several causes matter, though one or two often dominate.
A small number of general causes can explain most important behavior.
It depends heavily on the behavior.

decisions.reason: Direct items address substantial biological contribution; one twin vignette is excluded as general negative evidence.

construct.name: Biological causal attribution
construct.description: Weight assigned to biological and inherited causes of behavior.

candidateItems.text: Biological differences and inherited dispositions can make a substantial causal contribution to human behavior.
Biology contributes little to stable differences in human behavior compared with learning and social environment.
Identical twins raised apart show notable similarities in temperament despite very different environments. How much should this count as evidence for biological influence?

options.label: Strong evidence of biological contribution.
Some evidence, but not decisive.
Little evidence without ruling out other explanations.
No meaningful evidence for biological influence.

answerMeanings.proposition: Biological differences and inherited dispositions can substantially contribute to differences in human behavior.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
falsePositives: Caution about a single twin study is not denial of biological influence.

decisions.reason: Direct items address substantial environmental influence; one group vignette is excluded as general negative evidence.

construct.name: Environmental / social causal attribution
construct.description: Weight assigned to environmental, institutional, and social causes of behavior.

candidateItems.text: Many important human dispositions can change substantially when environments, incentives, and institutions change.
Social institutions and learned environments can strongly shape behavior even when biological differences are small.
People with similar biological dispositions can develop very different patterns of behavior when their social environments differ substantially.

Two groups with similar biological backgrounds grow up under very different institutions and develop sharply different norms and behavior. How much should this count as evidence for environmental influence?

options.label: Strong evidence that social environment can substantially shape behavior.
Some evidence, though other causes may also matter.
Little evidence without stronger causal controls.
No meaningful evidence for environmental influence.

answerMeanings.proposition: Social institutions and learned environments can substantially shape behavior.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
falsePositives: Caution about one comparison of groups is not denial of environmental influence.

construct.name: Agency theory family
construct.description: Derived but explicitly confirmed classification among compatibilist, libertarian, hard-determinist, skeptical, and related positions.

decisions.reason: The conditional items directly contrast agentic and impersonal divinity.

construct.name: Personal / agentic deity
construct.description: Degree to which divinity is understood as personal, intentional, or agentic.

candidateItems.text: If some divine reality exists, it is more likely to be capable of intentions than to be wholly impersonal.
Any divine reality that exists is more likely to be impersonal than to have intentions or preferences.

options.label: It is personal or agent-like, with intentions or purposes.
It has some mind-like or purposive aspects but is not simply a person.
It is fundamentally impersonal.
Its personal or impersonal character cannot be known.

answerMeanings.proposition: If divine reality exists, an intentional or personal character is more likely than a wholly impersonal one.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
falsePositives: Partly mind-like is not a fully personal deity.

decisions.reason: Two general possibility items address intervention; a single prayer case does not refute possibility.

construct.name: Divine / supernatural intervention
construct.description: Belief that supernatural agency intervenes in ordinary events.

candidateItems.text: A divine or supernatural agent can sometimes influence ordinary events in the world.
Even if supernatural reality exists, it does not intervene in ordinary events.
Someone prays for a specific outcome and an extremely unlikely event then occurs in exactly that way. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Divine or supernatural intervention is a live explanatory possibility.
Intervention is possible, but the event alone provides weak evidence.
The event should be explained entirely through natural causes or chance.
It depends on additional evidence about the event.

academicSources.title: Degelman & Lynn (1995): Belief in Divine Intervention Scale

answerMeanings.proposition: A divine or supernatural agent can sometimes influence ordinary events.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
nonEntailments: A particular event was an intervention
falsePositives: A natural account of one answered-prayer case does not rule out every intervention.

decisions.reason: Two general possibility items address miraculous events; an unexplained recovery is not a general test.

construct.name: Miraculous intervention
construct.description: Belief that events can occur through suspension or extraordinary override of ordinary natural regularities.

candidateItems.text: Events can sometimes occur through genuinely miraculous action rather than through ordinary natural processes alone.
All events occur through natural processes; genuinely miraculous events do not occur.

options.label: A genuine miracle is a live explanatory possibility.
An unknown natural explanation is more likely, though miracle is possible.
There must be a natural explanation even if current science has not identified it.
The case alone cannot distinguish miracle from unknown natural causes.

answerMeanings.proposition: Events can sometimes occur through miraculous action beyond ordinary natural processes.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.

decisions.reason: Overriding a purported revelation in one moral conflict does not deny all private revelatory authority.

A claimed revelation should not carry authority merely because it is sincerely believed to have a divine source.
A person believes a text is genuine divine revelation, but one teaching conflicts with their strongest independent moral judgment. Which should normally receive greater authority?

options.label: A: The believed revelation.
B: The independently reached moral judgment.

decisions.reason: Theism, deism, pantheism, and impersonal divinity are descriptive alternatives, not one direct scale.

construct.name: Divinity model
construct.description: Theistic, deistic, pantheistic, panentheistic, impersonal-divinity, and related models.

candidateItems.text: Which option is closest to your current view about divine reality?

options.label: At least one personal or agent-like God probably exists.
Some divine or sacred reality probably exists, but not as a personal agent.
I am substantially uncertain whether any divine reality exists.
Probably no divine reality exists.
No divine reality exists.

candidateItems.text: Which description is closest to your view of divine reality, assuming some divine reality exists?

options.label: A personal creator distinct from the universe.
A creator or ordering intelligence that does not normally intervene.
Divine reality is identical with the universe or nature as a whole.
The universe exists within divine reality but does not exhaust it.
Divine reality is fundamentally impersonal and not well described as a creator-person.

candidateItems.text: A divine creator could establish the universe and its laws without later intervening in events.
The natural universe itself may be appropriately identified with divine reality.
The universe may exist within a divine reality that is greater than the universe itself.
Divine reality need not be a person, mind, or creator in order to be genuinely divine.

decisions.reason: The non-designer possibility can be interpreted; choosing a divine source as most plausible does not make it necessary.

construct.name: Objective-purpose source
construct.description: Proposed source of objective meaning or purpose when such meaning is endorsed.

candidateItems.text: If human life has objective purpose, which source is most plausible?

options.label: A divine or cosmic intention.
Facts about human nature or flourishing.
Objective values or reasons that do not depend on a designer.
Objective purpose has no plausible source.

candidateItems.text: Objective purpose could exist because certain forms of human flourishing are objectively worth pursuing even without a divine designer.
Without some purposive mind or agent assigning a purpose, human life cannot have an objective purpose.

answerMeanings.proposition: A non-designer source of objective human purpose is a live plausible possibility.
answerMeanings.mixedBehavior: Both directional answers across authored units remain mixed/context-dependent.
nonEntailments: A divine reality does not exist
falsePositives: Choosing a nondivine source as most plausible does not establish objective purpose.

decisions.reason: A hypothetical without cosmic purpose cannot establish actual-world nihilism; nondivine objective meaning is another live view.

construct.name: Existential nihilism
construct.description: Degree of endorsement that life lacks objective or inherent meaning/value.

candidateItems.text: Human life has no objective meaning independent of what people create or value.
A human life can have objective meaning without being part of a cosmic or divine purpose.
Suppose there is no objective purpose built into human existence. Which is closest to your view?

options.label: Human life therefore lacks objective or inherent meaning.
Objective meaning could still arise from non-cosmic features of life.
Meaning can be created by persons even without objective purpose.
None of these descriptions fits well.

academicSources.title: The Meaning of Life (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

decisions.reason: World safety is an exploratory primal belief here; custom items are not a validated scale.

The world is fundamentally a dangerous place where serious threats are common.

construct.name: World aliveness / intentional character

decisions.reason: Existential orientation combines separately interpreted propositions.

construct.name: Response to meaninglessness

construct.name: Relational / interdependent self

options.label: Greatly; relationships and roles are partly constitutive of who the person is.

construct.name: Tolerance of otherness
construct.description: Acceptance of persons, lifestyles, and groups substantially different from one's own.

options.label: The society should protect their freedom to live that way.
The society should tolerate it but need not accommodate it.

decisions.reason: The direct group hierarchy item and matched hierarchy case align; justified-status wording is excluded.

construct.name: Distributive-principle family

candidateItems.text: Rank these distributive principles by how much weight they should usually receive when allocating important social resources.

options.label: Equality: distribute shares as equally as possible.
Need: give more to those with greater needs.

Sufficiency: ensure everyone reaches an adequate threshold first.
Priority: give extra weight to improving the position of those who are worse off.

Give extra weight to improving the position of those who are worst off.

contentFindings.finding: Both use frequent other-regarding behavior as evidence; they do not independently settle capacity for altruism.
The centralization mirror pair shares one authored unit and must not count as two independent answers.
Rankings do not independently identify equality, need, desert, sufficiency, priority, and entitlement.
The free-will items do not distinguish outright denial from incompatible theories of genuine control.
Relative property preference does not test whether commons could be legitimate alongside private ownership.
Deterrence as one aim, sufficient justification, and proportional limits need separate answer patterns.
Recognizing a textbook a priori example is not a report of worldview and remains excluded from public forms.
These combine distinct motivations, purposes, or descriptive and normative claims.
Hypothetical no-purpose and believed-genuine revelation conditions must not be treated as actual-world commitments.
Negating automatic authority, sufficient deterrence, or expertise alone does not assert the opposite broad proposition.
Workplace and technical-decision cases are context-bound and do not identify a partisan or universal governance position.
Possibility versus impossibility pairs are useful checks but should not be presented as psychometrically independent.
